text.brief: In May 1892 the Chinese Consolidated Benevolent Association in San Francisco told Chinese residents across the country not to register under a new federal law that required them to carry a certificate of residence.
text.record: The Chinese Exclusion Act of May 6, 1882, suspended the entry of Chinese laborers and barred Chinese immigrants from naturalization ([National Archives, Milestone Documents: Chinese Exclusion Act (1882)](https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/chinese-exclusion-act)). The Geary Act of 1892 extended the ban and required every Chinese laborer to carry a certificate of residence on pain of arrest and deportation ([Fong Yue Ting v. United States, 149 U.S. 698 (1893)](https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/usrep/usrep149/usrep149698/usrep149698.pdf); [State Department Office of the Historian: Chinese Immigration and the Chinese Exclusion Acts](https://history.state.gov/milestones/1866-1898/chinese-immigration)). The Supreme Court upheld the certificate in Fong Yue Ting v. United States in 1893, and Congress repealed exclusion only in December 1943 ([Fong Yue Ting v. United States, 149 U.S. 698 (1893)](https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/usrep/usrep149/usrep149698/usrep149698.pdf); [State Department Office of the Historian: Chinese Immigration and the Chinese Exclusion Acts](https://history.state.gov/milestones/1866-1898/chinese-immigration)).
text.reading: Exclusion turned ancestry into a legal category and built a federal registry to enforce it. That registry was the Data and Surveillance domain, and the United States ran it on its own residents. The guardrail in Military-Civil Fusion answers it directly. Ancestry is not loyalty.
